"Safe and Accurate Food Labeling Act" passes, prohibits states from enacting GMO-Labeling laws; allows FDA to include GMOs in definition of "natural"

Okay, so regardless of your position on GMOs, this is a huge states rights issue as well as a huge democracy issue. Formal surveys are showing 90% of Americans would like to at least know if the food they are buying is genetically modified or not.

I have a serious question I'm hoping somebody can break down for me - how exactly is this legal? As I understand it, states have the right to pass laws that are not specifically prohibited by a constitutional amendment. If I'm correct here, is there any chance what-so-ever this may be challenged and overturned?

Forcing manufacturers to label GMO food implies that there's something wrong with it. Arguments that start with "Regardless of how you feel, consumers should have the right to know..." sound good until you consider that one can make the same argument about anything. For instance, I can argue that I should have a right to know if any gingers have touched my food. Even if you don't believe that a ginger's lack of soul can leave a spiritual hex on foodstuffs, consumers should have the right to know if they're consuming food that has been touched by a daywalker. Why is Big Food refusing to inform the consumer? Are they trying to hide something?

I'd be much more supportive of an effort to label pesticide and herbicide use. One major use of GMOs is to create crops that are resistant to a major Monsanto herbicide, Ready Roundup. I don't care that corn is GMOd; I do care if said GMOd corn has been doused in Ready Roundup and only survived because it has the right gene. The issue there is the use of heavy herbicides and not the GMOing.

This. 137.4% this. It's like demanding to know if the food was harvested under the light of a full moon. It panders to inane fears and since it doesn't hold up to scientific scrutiny we need to face this as the issue it actually is. Too many people don't understand what actually makes a difference and are caring about entirely the wrong thing. I want to know what is being sprayed on the foods. I'm not giving organic farms a pass because I've seen the stuff approved for organic farming. I know that imported foods labeled as organic can have rotenone used on them (can only be used for killing fish in the US, but the restriction doesn't apply to produce grown outside of the US).

I was under the impression the majority of GMOs are for RoundUp resistance.

So you are starting on the premise that GMOs are unequivocally safe. I'm reserving judgement there. What is the most long-term study we have? What is the longest one we have without conflicts of interests.

Since we agree on the RoundUp labeling I want to point out that RoundUp was widely accepted as safe. It was advertised as targeting an enzyme "found in insects, but not in humans or plants," which was false and Monsanto is facing a lawsuit for it. Things we consider safe today - especially relatively new advents - can have new line shined on them in the future. I'm not saying GMOs are not safe, though I do have my doubts. I'm saying if my Tomatos have Flounder genes spliced into them (not making that up), I may want to make the personal choice to wait for more established science there, and I think that's my right. A small, text label on the back of the package where most consumers don't care to look anyway is not too much to ask for.
By the way, we force manufacturers to label plenty of things and that doesn't imply there's anything wrong with it. It could simply be listed under the ingredients for what it is.

Look at what went down in Europe. They put a label on GMOs which resulted in the market no longer providing GMOs in produce or as a commodity. Consumer preference was so compelled by the label that companies were pressured to not sell GMOs. Now Europeans have a lot less opinions for foods, smaller crop yields and higher prices for food.
It's scary how often states rights get squashed. As always, I don't see it as a food safety issue (current GMOs are safe) but states rights a precious.
States haven't had rights since the civil war.

Especially not after it has been found that all varieties of the sweet potato are naturally transgenic. That makes transgensis just as natural of a tool as selective breeding anyway.

Now a crop is either in a state otherwise found in nature, or it is in a state that only exists because it was bred, mutated, or transgenically created by man.

For me, if the DNA was manipulated manually (not by crossbreeding), then it's not natural anymore. If the DNA was changed just by breeding with other plants with the same tendency for the desired trait, then it's still natural.

The reason that plants can do photosynthesis is because they are transgenic with bacteria. Bacteria can take in a lot of foreign DNA or give it out, while plants can take in some DNA. If at the point where plants only exist because of something unnatural, how is anything natural?
